title: A Glance in the Cognitive Mirror: Validation of an Interpretation Bias Task  for Body Dissatisfaction
description: Interpretation biases (IBs) are thought to play a central role in body dissatisfaction (BD) and eating disorder (ED) psychopathology, yet validated assessment tools are limited. This study validated a newly developed German scenario based task (Body Dissatisfaction Interpretation Task; BDIT) designed to assess IBs in the context of BD. An online sample of cisgender women completed the BDIT and self report measures at two time points separated by 14 days (T1: N = 244; T2: N = 176). The task comprises 24 ambiguous everyday scenarios (distributed across three booklets) followed by BD related, negative non BD-related, and neutral interpretations. The BDIT demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = .85-.96), high test-retest reliability (ICC = .82-.91), and strong agreement across the three booklets (ICC = .83-.89). Convergent validity was supported by strong associations with BD and ED symptoms (r = .69-.79). Divergent validity was mixed, with weak correlations for unrelated constructs (alcohol consumption; spider anxiety; r = .10-.25), but moderate associations with anxiety‑related measures (agoraphobic cognitions; social anxiety, r = .44-.60), consistent with models conceptualizing IBs as partly transdiagnostic but showing graded specificity. The BDIT explained unique variance in BD beyond age, BMI, and ED symptoms, and showed a small, non-significant prospective effect over 14 days (β = .10, p = .092). These findings provide preliminary support for the BDIT as a reliable, valid, and easily implementable tool for assessing (changes in) IB in the context of BD, with potential applications in intervention studies evaluating cognitive change.

title: Reward Prediction Error Signaling as a Neurocomputational Correlate of Co-Occurring Anxiety and Depression in Youth
description: Co‑occurring depressive and anxiety symptoms (CADS) is a chronic and impairing condition that affects 1 in 6 youth. This underscores the need to identify neurocognitive mechanisms that characterize CADS. One candidate mechanism is altered reward prediction error (RPE), a reinforcement‑learning signal indexing the discrepancy between expected and received outcomes. Prior work has largely focused on RPE signaling in youth with anxiety or depression diagnoses, with limited attention to co‑occurring dimensional symptoms. To address this gap, we used computational modeling and neuroimaging to examine RPE‑modulated brain activation in relation to CADS. A transdiagnostic sample of 88 youths (Mage=14.43 years, range=8.81–18.57; 49% female) completed a child‑friendly two‑armed bandit reinforcement‑learning task during fMRI and completed anxiety and depressive symptom measures. Planned ROI‑based regressions and exploratory whole‑brain analyses tested the main and interactive effects of symptoms on RPE‑modulated activation in reward circuitry. ROI analyses showed no significant main effects of depressive symptoms, but parent‑reported anxiety was negatively associated with right amygdala RPE-modulated activation. Whole‑brain analyses identified three clusters with parent-reported symptoms: anxiety showed a positive association with RPE‑modulated activation in left superior frontal cortex, whereas depression was negatively associated with two clusters in left superior frontal and middle cingulate cortices. ROI‑based interactions indicated that elevated child‑ and parent‑reported CADS predicted RPE‑modulated activation in right ventral striatum and amygdala, respectively, such that positive associations between anxiety and RPE‑modulated activation weakened as depressive symptoms increased. Findings suggest that elevated CADS exert interactive, rather than additive, effects on RPE signaling.

title: Digital Companions for Academic Stress and Sleep Quality: A Conceptual Review and Developing Study with Primary Care Implications
description:
Post-secondary students continue to report high levels of academic stress, sleep disruption, and difficulty accessing timely mental-health support, all of which intersect with primary care. Artificial Intelligence (AI) companion chatbots are increasingly used by young adults because of their continuous availability and conversational design. Early digital mental-health research suggests these tools may support short-term mood regulation, coping, and perceived emotional support, although concerns remain regarding privacy, misinformation, and emotional over-reliance. This conceptual review examines current evidence on AI companion chatbots in relation to academic stress, student well-being, and early mental-health support pathways connected to primary care, while identifying key gaps and risks informing a developing master’s research study by Matthews. The review synthesizes literature across AI companions/chatbots, digital mental-health interventions, academic stress, and emerging student-use patterns, including evidence related to AI-mediated emotional support, stress regulation, academic self-efficacy, and foundational digital mental-health interventions demonstrating short-term improvements in mood and stress outcomes. Literature addressing risks, including privacy concerns, accuracy limitations, and emotional dependency, was also incorporated.

Findings from the conceptual review informed the design of a developing quantitative study examining how students perceive and use AI companion chatbots for stress management, sleep, coping, and help-seeking behaviors. Planned data collection includes pre- and post-surveys assessing academic stress, coping, sleep quality, and perceived well-being, alongside exploratory use of Matthews’ (2025) AI Companion Usage (AICU) Index to capture interaction patterns, motivations, and perceived relational qualities with AI companions. title: Social anhedonia predicts behavioral differences in young people with and without depression during social exchange
description:
The ability to form and sustain interpersonal relationships relies on the capacity to interpret social signals and update understanding of others’ behavior in dynamic contexts. Young adulthood is a critical period for refining these skills. Social learning and social reward responsivity have been implicated in depression, yet findings from social exchange studies remain mixed. Specifically, it remains unclear whether overall depressive symptom severity or specific symptoms such as anhedonia are most relevant to disrupted social decision-making.
In a single-session online study, we examined social learning and generosity sensitivity in a UK population sample of young adults (18–24 years; n=553). Participants completed the Social Learning–Generosity (SL-Gen) task, a multi-round trust game paradigm designed to probe feedback-driven updating and behavioral adaptation to structured generosity conditions, alongside questionnaire measures of depression (PHQ-9) and social anhedonia (ACIPS).
Depressive symptom severity was minimally associated with task performance; in contrast, greater social anhedonia and higher PHQ-9 anhedonia item scores were associated with differences in both evaluative updating and investment behavior. Specifically, individuals with greater social anhedonia showed lower initial investments, lower investments in higher generosity conditions, and smaller reductions in generosity ratings following unfair (loss-condition) interactions. Anhedonia was also associated with slightly flatter investment slopes in certain conditions.
These findings suggest that anhedonia, rather than global depressive symptom severity, is linked to reduced sensitivity to negative social feedback. Task-based social learning measures may therefore help identify mechanistic subgroups within depression characterized by blunted social reward processing which may have utility for pinpointing treatment targets.

title: Self-compassion and mental wellbeing: a baseline cross-construct map from a multilingual Erasmus+ youth-sector sample in Greece and France
description:
This is the companion paper to the design and feasibility evaluation of Compassion is Sexy (CIS), a 12–14 hour Erasmus+ KA210-YOU Small-scale Partnership compassion curriculum delivered across French-, Greek- and English-speaking workshop contexts during 2025–2026 (comPASSION is sexy, Project Code: 2024-3-FR02-KA210-YOU-000295806; no external research-ethics committee review; evaluation adheres to Erasmus+ quality standards for youth-sector practice). Where the intervention paper reports the dimensional pre–post pattern of change, the present analysis is restricted to the baseline phase and asks a single, prior question: how do the six factors of self-compassion relate to the three factors of mental wellbeing in this multilingual non-clinical adult sample?

The programme was delivered under the Erasmus+ KA210-YOU fewer-opportunities target framing; in 211 usable baseline participants (Greek site n = 105, including sizeable subgroups born outside Greece; French site n = 106, similarly multinational; roughly one third of respondents self-identified with at least one Erasmus+ fewer-opportunities or marginalised-status category), all six SCS-26 subscales were positively associated with the MHC-SF total (ρ = 0.18–0.34, all 95% CIs above zero except common humanity which crossed zero on the social cell). The strongest pooled pair was SCS total × MHC psychological (ρ = 0.42, CI [0.30, 0.52]). Across the 6×3 sub-by-sub matrix the pattern is selective rather than uniform: the self-relating SCS factors (self-kindness, self-judgmentR, isolationR, over-identificationR) load broadly across MHC dimensions, whereas the more cognitive-social SCS factors (common humanity, mindfulness) correlate reliably only with the psychological MHC dimension and show CIs that include zero for the emotional and social dimensions (Fig. 1, Table 1).

title: A short embodied compassion curriculum for the Erasmus+ youth sector: design, feasibility, and dimensional pre-post patterns of Compassion is Sexy in Greece and France.
description:
Compassion is Sexy (CIS) is a 12–14 hour, four-session experiential curriculum integrating self-compassion practices, embodied and arts-based methods, and group dialogue for mixed adult audiences (youth workers, facilitators, NGO staff, young adults) in non-formal Erasmus+ settings. The programme was delivered across French-, Greek-, and English-speaking workshop contexts during 2025–2026 in Greece and France within the Erasmus+ KA210-YOU Small-scale Partnership project comPASSION is sexy (Project Code: 2024-3-FR02-KA210-YOU-000295806). The evaluation was conducted within a low-risk, practice-based youth-work framework incorporating informed consent, voluntary participation, anonymisation, and data-minimisation procedures. This is an uncontrolled observational feasibility evaluation; pre–post statistics reflect within-person associations rather than causal effects.

From 288 intake records across 23 site-level CSV exports, 223 unique participants were identified after email-based linkage, of whom 211 had usable baseline data (Greece n = 105; France n = 106) and 56 returned a usable post-form (Greece n = 50; France n = 6; overall completion 27%). Participants completed the SCS-26 and MHC-SF. Scoring used item means with reverse coding for negative SCS items and 50% prorating thresholds for MHC subscales. One French cohort of five participants recorded no psychometrics due to placeholder export headers, and three English-language forms omitted MHC item 7.

At the headline level, the programme was associated with a moderate positive shift in total self-compassion (Mpre = 2.98, Mpost = 3.31; Cohen’s dz = 0.54, 95% CI [0.30, 0.85]) and a smaller positive shift in total mental wellbeing (dz = 0.42, CI [0.17, 0.70]); the Greek-only subsample closely tracked the pooled estimates. title: Higher individualism predicts lower intensity of experienced love: Data from 91 countries
description: Love is a near-universal human experience. However, while it transcends cultural boundaries, its intensity varies significantly across individuals and societies. We hypothesize that this variability is partly driven by socio-cultural factors, particularly individualism—a cultural orientation prioritizing personal goals over group interests. As individualism continues to rise globally, its implications for romantic relationships remain underexplored. Here, we address this by examining the link between individualism and love in two large-scale cross-cultural studies. In Study 1, we collected data from a convenience sample of 61,067 partnered individuals from 81 countries. In Study 2, we selected nationally representative samples from 50 countries, with controlled distributions of gender, age, and residential area (N = 6,620). The results were consistent across both studies—as individualism increased, both men and women reported lower levels of experienced love. In Study 2, individualism was additionally linked to a lower expressed desire for love, suggesting that individualism may erode the perceived importance of love. As people become increasingly individualistic, our findings provoke questions about the future of love. They also carry implications for societal challenges such as rising divorce rates, fertility issues, and depression—all of which have been linked to unfulfilled or unhappy love.

title: Systematic review: the integration and interpretation of Social Determinants of Health (SDH) in Digital Phenotyping research (DP)
description:
Background: Digital phenotyping (DP) for mental health is an emerging field with the potential to become a powerful tool in clinical settings. However, given the risk of bias or incorrect variable interpretation in marginalized subgroups, for this technology to be used effectively, social determinants of health (SDH) must be integrated into DP research. However it is not known how commonly and in what manner SDH are integrated into DP research. 
Methods: We conducted a systematic review of studies applying DP in mental health populations to examine how SDH variables are collected, reported, and integrated. The primary objective was to inform the development of practical, standardized guidelines for incorporating SDH into DP research. Eligible studies used DP in clinical populations defined as diagnosed, symptom-based, or at risk for mental health conditions. We excluded studies focused solely on chronic physical illness, age as a risk indicator, neurodegenerative conditions, or tobacco-only substance use, as well as reviews, protocols, and conceptual papers. We searched PubMed, Embase (OVID), and APA PsycInfo (OVID) on october 4th 2024, Web of Science Core Collection on  October 23rd 2024, and Scopus on October 24th, 2024. Studies were assessed for quality using the JBI Checklist and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). (PROSPERO ID: CRD42024626050).
Results: A total of 825 unique papers were screened at the abstract level, 192 underwent full-text review, 74 were accepted for data extraction, and 63 articles were ultimately included in the review.. Considerable heterogeneity was observed in how SDH were reported and integrated into digital phenotyping research. Age, sex, gender, and race/ethnicity were the most frequently reported variables, yet definitions were often inconsistent. title: The Functional Architecture of Self-Regulation: Network-Level Control Parameters of Regulatory Focus in Normative Adult and Adolescent Samples
description: Regulatory focus theory distinguishes promotion- and prevention-related motivational systems that support adaptive goal pursuit and are implicated in vulnerability to internalizing psychopathology. Prior neuroimaging work has characterized where in the brain these systems are instantiated, but has offered less insight into how they are organized as integrated control networks. We reanalyzed fMRI data from previously published normative adult (N = 48) and normative adolescent (N = 47) samples using a common region-of-interest framework derived from the adult activation maps. Three masks were constructed based on voxel-wise overlap across conditions: a core network capturing voxels active across multiple goal-priming conditions; a promotion-only network capturing promotion-selective processing; and a prevention-only network capturing prevention-selective processing. Within each mask, we derived per-subject parameters indexing system strength and signal differentiation for each motivational domain, and estimated cross-system coupling as the correlations among these parameters across individuals. In both age groups, promotion and prevention magnitudes varied largely independently, and within-system match–mismatch coupling was weak, consistent with a distributed architecture in which promotion and prevention share a representational backbone but operate with substantial differentiation. Adolescents showed significant cross-system coordination of match signals that was absent in adults. These findings support a set of network-level self-regulatory control parameters—strength, differentiation, and cross-system coupling—as a principled vocabulary for the functional architecture of regulatory focus specifically and self-regulation more generally, and provide a normative baseline against which perturbation by adversity, psychopathology, or intervention can be evaluated.

title: A cross-cultural psychometric evaluation of the 3-item Relationship Satisfaction Scale across 37 languages
description:
Objective: To advance research on close relationships, the present study provides a comprehensive psychometric evaluation of the 3-item Relationship Satisfaction Scale from the Perceived Relationship Quality Components (PRQC) inventory and assesses differences in relationship satisfaction across eight culturally and demographically diverse regions.
Background: Romantic relationships are among the most important social relationships humans form. The quality of these relationships shapes many aspects of life, ranging from everyday mood and behavior to health, long-term habits, longevity, and overall life satisfaction. Consequently, the scientific study of romantic relationship quality is of substantial importance. 
Method: Data from 49,876 participants recruited across 149 countries and territories were analyzed. Item-level properties, factor structure, item response theory (IRT) parameters, and measurement invariance, using both traditional approaches and the alignment method, across 37 linguistic versions of the scale were examined. Mean levels of relationship satisfaction were compared across major cultural and geographic regions using a two-level linear mixed-effects framework. 
Results: The findings indicate that the scale is reliable and broadly comparable across culturally diverse samples. All translated versions are publicly available on OSF (https://osf.io/47q6d/overview?view_only=ac5ba45cf89243e39f0a27e888d0fb9a). The results revealed cross-regional and cross-country differences in relationship satisfaction, with individuals from the English-Speaking region reporting the highest levels, while those from Confucian and African-Islamic regions reporting the lowest levels of relationship satisfaction.
Conclusion: Together, these results offer a strong methodological and conceptual foundation for advancing research on relationship quality and provide researchers with robust tools for studying relationship-related constructs across diverse populations speaking 37

title: Digital Traces of Everyday Smartphone Usage Predict Cognitive Ability
description: Scalable, objective judgments of individuals’ everyday cognitive functioning may facilitate decision making in key societal domains, including educational, occupational, and healthcare contexts. In a preregistered, theory-informed machine learning approach, we examine how digital traces of everyday smartphone usage allow for predictions of individuals’ general fluid intelligence (Gf), one of the most central human cognitive abilities. Leveraging a German quota sample (N = 367) providing smartphone sensing data of up to six months (1,269,491 phone usages), cross-validated results demonstrate that everyday smartphone usage consistently predicts individuals' Gf scores on a psychometric test (r_Md = .43, r_IQR  = [.35, .51]) with comparable criterion validity. High-dimensional combinations of behaviors (particularly short-term activities related to basic cognitive tasks and dealing with complexity) were predictive for Gf, highlighting how cognitive abilities manifest pervasively yet highly uniquely across individuals. The findings suggest that smartphone-based cognitive judgment may complement traditional cognitive assessments, enhancing early identification of cognitive functioning, fit, and support.

title: Evidence Before Entry: Evaluating the College of Psychologists and Behaviour Analysts of Ontario’s Regulation Modernization Proposals
description: This paper critically examines the proposed regulatory changes by the College of Psychologists and Behaviour Analysts of Ontario (CPBAO) to modernize entry-to-practice standards for psychologists and psychological associates in the province. The analysis places Ontario’s changing regulatory environment within the broader Canadian context, comparing provincial standards, training pathways, and workforce availability. Using empirical data, stakeholder feedback, and consensus reports, this manuscript examines evidence to test three implied hypotheses of the proposed changes: 1) they will increase the number of psychologists in Ontario, 2) they will improve access to mental health services, and 3) they will not elevate risk to public safety or reduce practitioner competence. Findings suggest that lowering entry standards and shifting from external accreditation to a college-approved process are unlikely to significantly increase access to mental health care. Evidence does not support the view that competence will remain unchanged among trainees from programs that substantially deviate from accredited models. Removing external evaluative safeguards may increase the likelihood that some less-prepared individuals enter independent practice. An evidence-based, data-driven approach grounded in transparent consultation and continuous evaluation is recommended to ensure that regulatory changes genuinely improve access to competent psychological care across both Ontario and Canada.

title: Meaningfulness Facilitates Voluntary Attentional Retrieval in Visual Working Memory
description: Visual working memory capacity benefits from stimulus meaningfulness, yet it remains unclear whether this advantage also enhances internal attention deployment. This study investigates whether voluntary and involuntary retrospective attention differentially prioritize meaningful (intact real-world objects) versus meaningless (diffeomorphically scrambled) representations. Two hypotheses were tested: (H1) involuntary attention preferentially selects meaningless representations, and (H2) voluntary attentional selection is facilitated by meaningful representations. Across two preregistered experiments, participants performed retro-cueing tasks manipulating cue type (voluntary vs. involuntary), stimulus type (intact vs. scrambled), and cue validity. Accuracy and reaction times were jointly modeled using hierarchical drift-diffusion models to dissociate representational quality (drift rate) from retrieval time (non-decision time). Experiment 1 used hemifield peripheral cues, while Experiment 2 employed single-item peripheral cues to maximize attentional deployment. Results showed that meaningful stimuli yielded higher drift rates, indicating enhanced representational quality. Voluntary attention produced robust retro-cueing effects (RCEs) on both drift rate and non-decision time. Critically, support for H2 emerged in non-decision time in Experiment 2, where the RCE was larger for intact than scrambled representations under voluntary attention. No such difference appeared in drift rate. By contrast, involuntary attention produced RCEs in drift rates but showed no reliable modulation by meaningfulness, providing inconclusive support for H1. These results suggest that although both attentional systems can prioritize internal representations, long-term memory selectively facilitates voluntary retrieval. Importantly, these findings highlight the need to dissociate decisional and non-decisional performance components, as semantic influences on attention emerge selectively in re

title: Differences in Dishonesty Toward Humans and Artificial Agents: The Role of Agent Type and Pupil Size
description: As artificial agents become more involved in social and economic interactions that rely on honest behavior from humans, they are increasingly designed with human-like social cues, such as pupil size, to appear more approachable. Pupil size is subtle, but also a powerful cue that can guide our decisions. Yet, we still know little about how pupil size shapes people’s behavior, especially across cultures where agents and their signals are interpreted and accepted differently. In this study, 275 participants from Europe and Japan played a coin toss game where lying increased financial gain. They interacted with a human confederate, a virtual avatar, or a robot. Agents' pupil sizes were manipulated to appear large or small; for human confederates, this was achieved using custom-designed contact lenses. Our results suggest that cultures differ in how dishonest behavior is directed toward human and artificial agents: European participants were more dishonest toward artificial agents than toward humans, while Japanese participants showed no such differentiation across agent types. Beyond this, pupil size influenced dishonesty specifically towards avatars in culture-specific ways, with European being more honest towards avatar with small pupils compared to large, and the opposite pattern for Japanese participants. Exploratory analyses further revealed cultural differences in mind perception attributions across agent types, alongside overlapping pupillary responses towards agents across cultures. These findings highlight the need to consider cultural context when designing artificial agents that use human-like cues to guide social behavior: what subtly communicates warmth in one culture may signal something else in another.

title: Accumulation, transfer, and maturation in bilingual toddlers’ word learning
description: Bilingual children typically must learn two labels for each concept they encounter, one in each language, effectively doubling the number of words they acquire relative to monolinguals. While bilinguals typically know fewer words in each language than monolinguals, they do not show the delay that would be expected if learning double the words required double the time. Three mechanisms may explain this: the accumulation of language-specific experience with labels (operationalized as language-adjusted word frequency), transfer across and within languages, and maturational changes in learning efficiency. The present studies investigate the interplay of these factors using computational simulations (Study 1) and models of empirical data from toddlers aged 16-30 months acquiring English and/or French (Study 2). Simulations progressively incorporated language exposure and transfer between translation equivalents, establishing that accumulator models require some degree of transfer to produce realistic bilingual vocabulary trajectories. Empirical models first replicated accumulator models with monolingual data, then extended them to bilinguals, confirming that concept frequency, language exposure, and age all predicted word learning, with age emerging as the strongest predictor and modulating the effects of the other two. Moreover, in bilingual children, concept frequency was a stronger predictor of word production than language-adjusted word frequency. Language exposure also independently predicted word production, suggesting that broader language experience supports acquisition beyond the accumulation of experience with individual labels. These findings indicate that accumulation, transfer (both cross-language and within-language), and maturation interact, enabling bilingual children to learn words from two languages without requiring twice the experience.

title: The Impact of Mood and Affective Priming on Art Evaluation:  A Systematic Literature Review
description:
Many studies in empirical aesthetics investigate emotional responses to art. Yet the role of affective states that precede an encounter with art remains surprisingly underexamined. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on how affective priming, experimentally induced mood, as well as baseline mood shape the evaluation of visual art. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PsycINFO, Scopus, and PubMed (1970–2025), yielding 68 records. Eight studies met inclusion criteria, and seven additional studies were identified via backward citation tracking and supplementary searches, resulting in 15 quantitative studies (N = 1,600).
Across studies, affective influences were categorized as affect-congruent, affect-incongruent, arousal-related, or context-dependent. Overall, preceding affect can modulate core evaluative outcomes such as liking, beauty, interest, and sublimity, but effects are heterogeneous. Several priming paradigms show affect-congruent shifts in liking, whereas other studies report affect-incongruent enhancements (e.g., fear increasing sublimity or negative primes increasing beauty). Induced mood findings further suggest sensitivity to the specific induction method (e.g., clearer evaluation shifts for text-based, self-focused inductions than for film clips). Baseline mood effects appear more conditional and context-dependent, emerging most clearly when contextual information or task demands invite open elaboration. 
We map the evidence onto Forgas’s Affect Infusion Model (AIM), arguing that variability across findings is interpretable in terms of judgment strategies (heuristic vs. substantive vs. motivated processing) and corresponding routes of affect integration. We conclude with methodological priorities and future directions aimed at directly testing mechanisms and embodied pathways through which affect shapes aesthetic evaluation.

title: Limits to intuition in number compositionality:  the case of multiplicative commutativity
description: Commutativity—the principle that operand order does not affect the result of an operation—is a core feature of two foundational operations of arithmetic: addition and multiplication. Recent theories propose that such compositional structures emerge from an innate “language of thought” that enables abstract principles to apply flexibly across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. While children possess early intuitions about additive commutativity, less is known about their grasp of the commutativity of multiplication. Here, we ask whether children’s understanding of the commutative principle of multiplication stems from pre-existing intuitions that the order in which sets are grouped does not matter, or whether it instead emerges from reasoning about structural relations among numerical symbols. We tested 8- to 9-year-old children in a number comparison game, probing their understanding of multiplicative commutativity in both symbolic expressions (3x2 = 2x3) and in non-symbolic sets of grouped dots. On average, children performed better with symbolic expressions than with non-symbolic arrays. Moreover, their performance on the arrays of grouped dots was directly linked to their mastery of commutativity in symbolic expressions, and independent of their intuitive, non-symbolic numerosity estimation skills. To probe children’s developing mastery of the commutativity of multiplication, a subset of the children were given brief training on commutativity and played the same game in a second session, 2 to 14 days later. Children who, in the first session, did not master the commutative principle with symbolic stimuli showed improvement on symbolic trials, while improvement on non-symbolic trials lagged for the entire group. These findings suggest that symbolic learning of the principle of commutativity of multiplication comes first, before children can apply it to concrete contexts. Moreover, they provide evidence for format- and operation-specific limits to children’s master

title: Cross-Linguistic Factors in Early Numerical Development
description: What role does language play in exact numerical reasoning? We argue that natural language represents number at multiple levels that vary cross-linguistically – in grammatical morpho-syntax, in number words, and in rule-governed counting routines. In this chapter, we first describe how cross-linguistic variability in grammatical structure impacts our representations of countable individuals and sets (Part I). Next, we review variability in how languages represent small numbers (Part II). And finally, we describe cross-linguistic variability in the syntactic structure of counting systems (Part III). We suggest that cross-linguistic research provides an important window into how humans come to reason about exact magnitudes, and conclude with a discussion of outstanding questions and avenues for future research.

title: “I know who the bad guy is!” Infants map the word “bad” to hinderers, but not the word “good” to helpers
description: Though a wealth of research has found that young infants have the capacity to evaluate helping and hindering agents (e.g. Hamlin, 2007; for a review, see Woo et al., 2025), it is nevertheless unclear whether these evaluations reflect mere social evaluations or more mature understanding of moral concepts. The present experiments probed the nature of infants’ evaluations by testing whether they associate the morally-relevant words “good” and “bad” with helpers and hinderers. In Exp.1, 32 19-month-olds watched a live puppet show where a protagonist puppet is either helped or hindered by another puppet (ball show, adapted from Hamlin & Wynn, 2011). Then, the infant was presented with the helper and hinderer puppets, and asked, “can you point to the good/bad guy?”. Results revealed that whereas infants reliably mapped “bad” to the hinderer (24/31, p = .003), they showed relatively inconsistent mapping of the word “good” to the helper (p = .09). In Exp.2, 42 20-month-olds watched a video recording of the ball show, then engaged in a preferential looking paradigm in which still images of the helper and hinderer were shown on the screen. An audio prompt then asked, “Where’s the good/bad guy? Find the good/bad guy,” while an eye-tracker monitored infants’ gaze. Results paralleled and bolstered that of Exp.1: infants looked significantly longer at the hinderer when hearing the “bad” prompt, but looked equally at both characters when hearing the “good” prompt. Together, these findings suggest that infants may associate the abstract moral word “bad” with hindering behaviour prior to the second birthday, but the association between “good” and helping behaviour may emerge later. This asymmetry provides further evidence for a negativity bias in social cognition.

title: Using Natural Language Processing to Study Scene Recall in 360° Virtual Reality
description: This study examines how viewing scenes in 2D versus 3D 360° virtual reality affects recall of those scenes. Participants will view immersive scenes presented in both formats and later provide verbal descriptions of what they remember. These recall narratives will be analyzed using natural language processing to examine how the shift from 2D to 3D influences the amount, type, and organization of remembered scene information. The main goal is to determine whether 3D immersive viewing leads to richer or more detailed scene recall compared with 2D viewing. Natural language processing methods will be used to quantify features of participants’ descriptions, including references to objects, spatial layout, actions, perceptual details, and overall descriptive richness. This allows the study to assess not only how much participants remember, but also what kinds of scene information are most affected by the viewing format. By combining 360° virtual reality with computational language analysis, this project aims to better understand how an immersive visual experience shapes memory for complex scenes. The findings may help clarify whether 3D presentation enhances scene encoding and recall, and how these effects are reflected in the language people use to describe remembered environments.

title: Evaluating the Residualized Change Score Pretest-Posttest Mediation Model via the Latent Change Score Specification
description: Researchers frequently use statistical mediation analysis to better understand the possible mechanisms through which change occurs in pretest-posttest designs. One common approach is the residualized change score model, in which the posttest mediator and outcome measures are regressed on their pretest values and residuals are used as variables in the mediation model. When implemented with a latent change score (LCS) specification for structural equation modeling, this model is typically estimated with a two-step procedure: posttest-pretest slopes are calculated first and then treated as fixed in the subsequent model. Valente et al. (2021) found that the standard implementation produced conservative Type I error rates, which we successfully replicated. Rates often fell below the lower bound of the recommended robustness interval for the chi-square test. We explore two possible solutions: a df-adjusted model (recalculating fit statistics with 2 fewer df) and a one-step model (estimating the slopes within the LCS model). Through a Monte Carlo simulation, these adjustments are compared against the standard implementation. The df-adjusted model often yielded high Type I error rates. The one-step model produced the closest Type I error rates to the nominal 0.05 and produced more accurate model fit statistics. This one-step procedure is recommended when estimating the residualized change score model to ensure that mediation findings are based on a properly specified model and valid statistical inferences.

title: Beyond Valence: Arousal as a Core Dimension of Affective Polarization
description: Although affective polarization is fundamentally an affective construct, existing theories and measures focus almost exclusively on evaluative valence, largely overlooking emotional arousal. Building on the Circumplex Model of Affect, we develop and evaluate a two-dimensional framework of affective reactions toward political parties and affective polarization that incorporates emotional valence and arousal. Across three studies conducted in the Netherlands (N=984), the United Kingdom (N=1,001), and the United States (N=1,000), we show that feeling thermometers function as measures of valence and that valence and arousal represent empirically distinct dimensions of affective reactions. We then demonstrate that the level of emotional arousal provides incremental validity over traditional, valence-based measures of affective polarization, yielding additional and often stronger associations with key political correlates such as political engagement, ideological extremity, and democratic attitudes. These findings advance the conceptualization and measurement of affective polarization by incorporating arousal as a distinct dimension and clarifying when and why affective polarization is most strongly linked to political behavior and democratic attitudes.

title: Socially Motivated Observational Learning: Children Preferentially Learn from Overheard Speech Addressed to Their Own Mothers
description: When does overheard speech support early word-learning? The present study provides preliminary evidence that children’s closest social partners (here, mothers) structure attention to overheard speech. In a Tseltal Mayan community where overhearing is central to socialization, 75 mother-child dyads participated in overhearing-sessions exposing them to two novel words. In each session, one child’s mother was directly addressed (“Mother-Addressed” condition), while the second mother merely observed (“Mother-Unaddressed” condition). Immediately after, both children completed two gaze-based tests of word recognition and learning. Results show that, compared to Mother-Unaddressed children, Mother-Addressed children exhibited (i) greater one-shot recognition of the novel word whose referent was visible during the overhearing-session; and (ii) a word-learning advantage on cross-situational familiarization trials . Insofar as who is being spoken to matters, the present study finds that not all overheard input is created equal: rather, results provide preliminary evidence that observational word-learning is socially-structured.

title: Tiny Alchemists: The Developmental Emergence of Empowerment in Exploration
description: How do children's exploration strategies develop? Prior work has shown that children explore more broadly than adults, often driven by uncertainty. Yet, little is known about how more sophisticated strategies, such as empowerment - i.e. seeking actions that expand future possibilities - unfold across development. We investigated this in two experiments using a complex combinatorial game ("Tiny Alchemy''). In Experiment 1, we found that empowerment use increased with age, while uncertainty decreased. Young children (5 - 8 years) primarily relied on uncertainty, while older children (9 - 13 years) and adults used both uncertainty and empowerment. In Experiment 2, we asked whether younger children's limited use of empowerment reflected different semantic intuitions. Results showed that older children used empowerment but could not explicitly judge it, while adults both used and accurately assessed empowerment. These findings suggest that empowerment emerges gradually: first as an implicit strategy in late childhood, and only later becoming explicit and verbalizable.

title: From Agent-Based Opinion Models to Quantum Circuits: A Tutorial
description:
This work describes and assesses fundamental quantum computing concepts from the perspective of the social sciences. Quantum computers differ fundamentally from classical computers in that their elementary units, qubits, can exist in superpositions of multiple states simultaneously. This
property makes them particularly suited for simulating systems with a large number of interacting components, a promising perspective across disciplines.
In this tutorial, we introduce (i) what properties a social dynamic model should have to be easily translatable into quantum computer mechanics, (ii) eleven steps that have to be completed to achieve that translation and (iii) a practical example in which we illustrate the process.

title: Volitional Meditative Absorption States in an Advanced Yogic Practitioner: A Neurophenomenological EEG Study
description: Advanced meditative absorption states remain difficult to study scientifically because they are rare, challenging to elicit under controlled conditions, and depend strongly on first-person phenomenology. This study presents a neurophenomenological case report of an advanced Yogic meditator with more than 20 years of sustained practice who reliably entered a deeply absorbed state referred to by the participant as the “Silent Mind” state and interpreted within the framework of Yogic samādhi. Across four independent EEG recording days, the participant repeatedly entered and exited the state using self-marked onset and offset triggers. High-density 64-channel EEG was recorded together with ECG and respiration. Phenomenological reports described a state of profound inner silence, absence of discursive thought and mental imagery, preserved clarity of awareness, and a vertically organized internal experiential structure. EEG analyses revealed a reproducible temporal sequence: rapid suppression of alpha-band activity at state onset, delayed amplification of infra-slow activity, and increases in gamma-band power during sustained absorption. Power spectral density analyses further showed marked attenuation or near-removal of the alpha peak during meditation segments, while band-power comparisons indicated increases in infra-slow and gamma activity and alpha suppression relative to baseline. These findings suggest that the recorded absorption state was associated with a distinct multiscale electrophysiological reconfiguration rather than resembling a simple extension of relaxed wakefulness or focused attention. Although conclusions remain limited by the single-case design and the interpretative nature of traditional state classification, this study demonstrates the feasibility and scientific value of combining repeated state sampling, high-density EEG, and detailed phenomenological documentation in the investigation of advanced meditative absorption.

title: Partial Metric Invariance in the Latent Actor-Partner Interdependence Model: A Simulation Study Evaluating the Performance of Four Analytical Approaches
description: When modeling interdependence between two individuals using the latent Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (the latent APIM), metric invariance is essential but often only partially achieved in practice. This paper evaluates four analytical approaches under partial metric invariance: sum scoring, full-invariance modeling, partial-invariance modeling, and invariance-ignoring modeling. For the latter two approaches, we further examine the impact of misspecifying noninvariant items. Results show that sum scoring yielded biased estimates, whereas the other three approaches produced accurate standardized estimates. Invariance-ignoring modeling was most robust to misspecification regarding unstandardized estimates. These findings offer practical guidance for researchers modeling dyadic interdependence with latent constructs.

title: Short words are more likely to refer to multiple meanings across 192 language families
description: This study tested, for the first time on a diverse cross-linguistic dataset, the existence of a negative correlation between a word’s length and its semantic ambiguity. This correlation can be predicted on various grounds: as a way to make communication more efficient, as a mechanical consequence of the greater availability of short wordforms, or as a corollary of Zipf’s laws of abbreviation and meaning, which state that frequent words are shorter and have more meanings. We tested the correlation between word length and number of meanings in a broad range of languages, our biggest analysis studying 633,308 wordforms in 1,952 languages representing 192 families. We operationalise word ambiguity in three ways: as whether or not a word colexifies several meanings, using Lexibank data, as the number of synsets in Wordnet, and using BERT-derived predictions of the degree of ambiguity of a word. For all three measures of ambiguity, we evidence a robust correlation between a word’s brevity and ambiguity. The correlation remains substantial when controlling for word frequency, suggesting that it is more than a by-product of the fact that frequent words tend to be both shorter and more ambiguous.

title: Goals shape dynamics of attention and selection for value-based decision-making
description: Humans can flexibly adjust how they make decisions to arbitrary goals. However, most theories in decision-making focus on predicting one specific choice type (i.e., choosing the best option). Here, we link decision-making and cognitive-control research to test a theory that accounts for flexible adjustments of choice mechanisms to different goals and demands. Our biologically inspired model specifies how different features translate into evidence for the current goal, and how evidence is mapped onto different output structures. We tested the model in an eye-tracking study in which participants were asked to choose one out of four consumer products or to appraise the entire set, each with respect to positive or negative value. The results confirmed our preregistered hypotheses that response time (RT) should decrease with the overall value of a set of options in choose-best but increase in choose-worst trials. As predicted, this interaction was absent in appraisal RT, which instead exhibited an inverted-U-shaped pattern. Furthermore, the amount of attention devoted to an option was positively related to its value in choose-best, negatively related in choose-worst trials, and unrelated when participants appraised entire sets of products. Time-resolved analyses of eye movements revealed strategic goal-dependent search processes, as attention is increasingly focused on goal-congruent options in choice but remains more uniformly distributed in appraisal. Our findings suggest that cognitive control shapes choice and search dynamics by flexibly adjusting them to current goals and demands.
